Field Report—Day 19  
  
After two weeks at sea, we finally made landfall in Castora. Nearly lost my damn life on the Martingale with the Blood tribune. Anyone's guess as to why I thought I was safer with a first-time captain instead of with the practiced corsairs.  
  
But now? My paws are firmly planted on solid ground. Grateful for that.  
  
So far, my surveillance of the outer and inner shores has been...enlightening. There's not much I've seen so far that would be of much use to the legions. Though with the various castaway groups here, I've no shortage of small societal intrigue. Folks who want to leave, folks who want to stay, freebooters harassing Hullgardeners, some weird cult, and the Inquest.  
  
I'll tuck this someplace dry for now and go skulking. Maybe grab one of those fruity beverages from the bar. Before I left, Malice joked it'd been a while since I'd taken downtime when she assigned me to this expedition. Guess I should take the hint...

Determining whether to aid crash survivors is all about risk assessment. First, always avoid approaching a castaway alone or without a weapon. They just went through hell... May not be in the mood for conversation.  
  
Never hesitate to return to Hullgarden for backup, but if you choose to proceed, stay alert. Watch for freebooters, too; it's possible you could be walking into a trap set by our rivals. If it's not a freebooter trap, they're not far behind. They'll try to beat us to any cargo that washes ashore, so they're bound to show up sooner or later.  
  
Once the coast is clear and you've determined that the castaway is friendly, bring them to me. All newcomers should be seen by Westergard or myself before getting too comfortable.  
  
And remember—don't risk your life for a few crates of stale bread. Never do cargo retrieval without a full party.  
  
Mayor Osborne

My pride, my pupil. For you, I leave my instructions, my wishes, and my words of affirmation. There are few among my stewards that can truly thread the weave of magic that flows through this place, that possess the knowledge of creation as you do. Perhaps that is why I chose to impart to you and some of your siblings a spark of mortal pathos. In part to see if it could be done, but also knowing that it would be imperative for your role at the forge.  

As this chapter of my life comes to a close, my hope is that you will one day come to appreciate the act of creation and the value of congregation. It is a shortcoming of many seers, I have noticed, to attempt to carry the most lofty burdens of our elevated society on their solitary shoulders, becoming islands unto themselves.  

Put those ideas far from your mind, my pupil. For I say, whether by mortal hand or machine, we cannot make the future alone. Lean on the other stewards, on future artificers, and build things that fill you with the same satisfaction I feel looking at you now. There will be times that you will falter, as we all do, but you will also learn and grow, and, if you have followed my advice, you will have done so together.  

—Gardesano

*A single excerpt of the book remains legible.*   
  
**ADVISORY: This text has been delisted by the table of the arch-steward for seditious material. It is not approved for distribution. Existing copies are recommended for immediate destruction.**  
    
**Persons found in possession of unauthorized literature are subject to penalty, including but not limited to: fines, detention, transportation, execution, and community service.**    
   
...It was the silence, Junon realized. It should have tipped him off.     
  
*Damn fool*, he thought to himself, wings flexing on instinct. *A fine mess you've gotten into this time*. The seer trap had sprung before he could register its presence woven into the stone below him. It had been subtle. Pragmatic. Nearly mursaat.    
  
The blue tendrils of magic binding him held fast, pinning him flush against the cold wall of the ritual antechamber. Shadowcraft? No; too reckless while the mirror network remained throttled. The Hidden Wings could no longer be trusted, either. Improvisation was the name of the game, now...and Junon's life would be the collateral.    
  
For the moment, he affected a casual lack of concern. His attention turned to his seer captor.   
  
Viaro the Tragedian regarded Junon with a cold kind of satisfaction, two of his four arms folded behind his back. The other two arms occupied themselves with the shadowstone dagger, as though mocking Junon for ever believing the relic would be left so carelessly unguarded.   
  
His old friend Viaro. Who else could it have been? Deadly as any seer assassin. Twice as prideful.   
  
"You're slipping," Viaro remarked lightly. The corner of his mouth betrayed his excitement.   
   
Junon kept his own voice light. "So are you," he said. He returned the smile, hidden though it lay beneath his mask. "An invisibility hex? One of ours, I suspect. I thought subterfuge anathema to your kind."   
   
"Failure is anathema," Viaro hissed. His face was close now, all lines and deep angles. "My fhogos shall do whatever it takes to save this world from your vile chaos."   
  
"Will you?" Junon breathed.   
   
Viaro's fingers found purchase on the facets of Junon's mask.    
   
With each clasp undone, Junon's mind wandered. How many centuries had they known one another? How many of Viaro's forces had Junon killed? How many of Junon's forces had fallen to Viaro? In the end, only they were left standing, the two constants in the deadly calculus of war between their peoples.   
  
When Viaro's hands withdrew, Junon's mask followed. For the very first time, they knew each other fully. Eye to eye.   
   
"There you are," whispered the Tragedian.   
   
For a moment they stood there, silent. A fleeting eternity.    
    
*The page is torn away at the bottom. The messy nature of the tear implies passion.*
